title: Nothing fixed (section 7)
hookLine: has the Tathagata attained anything? there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening

lines: THE REFLEX ANSWER: YES AND YES.
cards: A test question, with a trap folded inside. The Buddha asks Subhuti two things. Has the Tathagata attained the highest, complete awakening?
And has the Tathagata taught any teaching? Anyone in that room could answer on reflex: yes, and yes. That's the whole story, isn't it?
A seeker sits under a tree, wakes up, and spends his life teaching what he found. But Subhuti has been listening to this sutra, and he answers more carefully than that.

teach.b: First, the question. In the sutra's Sanskrit, that awakening has a long, grand name: anuttara samyak sambodhi, awakening that's complete, with nothing above it. Second, Subhuti's answer.

As I understand what the Buddha has taught, he says, there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening, and no fixed teaching that the Tathagata has taught. No fixed thing: that's the phrase to hold, lightly.
What the Tathagata has taught, Subhuti says, can't be grasped and can't be spoken. It isn't a thing, and it isn't a no-thing either.
Then a short line closes the section: the wise and holy ones are all set apart by the unconditioned, by what isn't put together from parts. Fourth, what this is not saying.
It isn't saying the Buddha never woke up, or taught nothing, or that the teaching is empty talk. The rest of the sutra is a teaching, after all, and Subhuti is learning from it.

teach.h: NOT AN OBJECT IN A POCKET.
teach.b: It's saying awakening isn't an object he picked up and put in his pocket, something with edges you could hand over. Waking up in the morning isn't something you keep in a drawer, either.
The same goes for smaller certainties. I'm the responsible one. She never listens.
This job is who I am. Each one is useful.
Held as a fixed thing, each starts to harden. The sutra keeps the hand open, even around the highest thing it knows.

how: Teachers in Mahayana schools, Zen among them, use this section to point out that awakening is not a possession to be gained.

o: the teaching is empty talk with no real meaning
awakening isn't a thing to grasp, pocket or hand over
the Buddha never truly woke up under the tree

p: has he attained the highest awakening?
can't be grasped, can't be spoken

s: Subhuti says the Buddha never woke up
he says there's no fixed thing called the highest awakening, not that there's no awakening.
in this section, what the Tathagata taught is said to be neither a thing nor a no-thing
it can't be grasped and can't be spoken.
the sutra says the teaching is empty talk
the sutra is itself a teaching, and Subhuti is learning from it.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: has the Tathagata attained the highest awakening, and has he taught any teaching? what do you answer?
o: yes and yes: that's the whole story.
there's no fixed thing called awakening, and no fixed teaching.
no: the Buddha attained nothing and taught nothing.
games.why: Subhuti says there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening and no fixed teaching: what was taught can't be grasped or spoken, and is neither a thing nor a no-thing.

practice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and bring to mind one thing you're sure of, about yourself or someone close to you. Notice how you're holding it, like a fist or like water in cupped hands.
You don't have to drop it or argue with it; just let the grip ease by one degree, the way your palms are already open.

wordCard.voice: Nothing fixed. There is no fixed thing called the highest awakening, and no fixed teaching; what the Buddha taught can't be grasped. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: unsurpassed, complete awakening; the sutra's name for what the Buddha awoke to.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing fixed. Not even the highest awakening fits in a pocket. Until tomorrow.
